newsitem.title: USA: FUND VIEW - Investors leave techs, love big-caps.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Investors leave techs, love big-caps.

text.p: Investors have fallen out of love with volatile small-capitalization and technology mutual funds, and have sought refuge in more conservative growth and income and index funds, fund analysts said Friday.
"There is clearly a move away from funds that invest primarily in technology and small-cap stocks," said Robert Adler, president of AMG Data Services, which tracks funds.
Emerging growth, or small cap, funds had net redemptions of $296 million for the week ended April 16, versus inflows $965 million for the week of April 9, according to AMG.
Adler found that assets in the emerging growth sector have dropped 10 percent to $113 billion for the latest week from $125 billion in February.
The technology sector suffered net redemptions of $57 million versus redemptions of $151 million for the previous week. The sector has had redemptions in eight of the last 10 weeks, Adler said.
AMG estimated the growth and income sector had hefty inflows of $1 billion, about the same level as the previous week.
AMG noted, for example, that the Vanguard Index 500 fund, the second largest fund in the United States, collected $172 million in new assets for the week.
While Vanguard declined to confirm the data, a spokesman said the flows "have been strong and positive."
The spokesman added, "Growth and income has been enjoying considerably higher cash inflows than aggressive growth funds for the last couple of week."
Another robust sector was international funds, which recorded inflows of $618 million compared with inflows of $697 million for the previous week.
"Those are big numbers," said Adler. "Flows have been steadily rising now for the last five weeks."

For the month through April 16, Charles Schwab Corp tallied $5 million in net redemptions in aggressive growth funds, with net buys of $142 million in international funds, net buys of $132 million in index funds and net buys of $59 million in growth and income, according to spokesman Glen Mathison.
The data represents all third mutual funds sold by Schwab.
Analysts noted that money has continued to broadly pour into stock funds, although more slowly, even as the major stock indices have declined in the past few weeks.

The amount of money flowing into stock funds for the week ended April 16 slowed to $1.6 billion from $4.1 billion inflows for the previous week and $5.2 billion for the same week last year, according to AMG.

"Even with the market down eight of the last nine weeks before this week, there is still new money going into conservative funds," said Charles Biderman, president of Mutual Fund Trim Tabs. "They've been the best performers. Investors usually invest with their eyes on the rear view mirror."
According to the latest data from Lipper Analytical Services, growth and income funds and index funds were the only two performance winners among equity funds for the week ended Thursday.
Growth and income returned 0.15 percent, while index gained 0.47 percent. All other equity sectors retreated.
Wall Street firms are helping to encourage the shift to large-cap funds by beating the drum for the stocks that the funds buy.

Predicting that these shares will generally continue to outperform the market over the next 12 to 24 months, Travelers Group Inc's Smith Barney equity strategist John MacNeil said: "...Large-cap growth stocks will once again regain ascendancy, when overall earnings growth slows either of its own accord or with some help from higher interest rates, courtesy of the Fed."
